key_claims: USAID and other agencies routinely overstated positive results in education, health and women's programs without verifiable evidence.
SIGAR's Lessons Learned Program was launched in 2014 to provide institutional memory against the 'annual lobotomy' of personnel rotations.
Over $133 billion has been spent on Afghan reconstruction, including more than $70 billion on security forces and about $9 billion on counternarcotics.
The 2013 U.S. rule-of-law strategy for Afghanistan had no performance measures, versus 27 in the 2009 strategy.
The Taliban filled the void in districts vacated by coalition forces by 2014, outcompeting Afghan forces and civil servants.
SIGAR concluded that reintegration programs did not weaken the insurgency or reduce violence and should resume only after a peace agreement.
Counternarcotics efforts failed to produce lasting reductions in poppy cultivation, and drug money continued to flow to insurgent groups.
The US spent over $70 billion on an ANDSF that could not provide nationwide security.
Corruption undermined the US mission from the start of Operation Enduring Freedom.
The US inadvertently aided the Taliban's resurgence by allying with warlords whose abuses drove Afghans toward the Taliban.
SIGAR says unchecked corruption, abetted by US spending, undermined strategic goals.
US aid to Afghanistan exceeded 45 percent of GDP by 2004 and over 100 percent in 2007 and 2010.
SIGAR warns a peace deal with the Taliban requires planning, including reintegrating an estimated 60,000 Taliban fighters.
US personnel sent to Afghanistan often did not know the difference between al-Qaeda and the Taliban.
SIGAR found the State/USAID and DoD responses did not provide the requested ten most/least successful projects.
SIGAR argued national-level indicators lack causal links to specific US programs.
SIGAR noted USAID's agriculture program ignored poppy eradication goals, with increased poppy cultivation in covered provinces.
SIGAR said ANSF illiteracy (86% in 2009) and turnover limit what literacy training numbers show.
School construction crowded out operations and maintenance funding per the World Bank.
SIGAR argues agency indicators lack credible links between outputs and outcomes, e.g. in education, anticorruption and counternarcotics.
DOD and State/USAID responses did not address sustainment of Afghan government capacity beyond limited examples.
State/USAID say they evaluate projects against their own initial standards and do not compare projects.
USAID alternative-development program was directed away from poppy eradication goals, with opium cultivation rising in covered provinces.
State and USAID claim measurable gains in education, health, revenue and women's roles since 2001.
The letter acknowledges fraud, delays, contractor overcharges and insecurity as constant features of assistance in Afghanistan.
USAID ended the Strategic Provincial Roads project in fall 2011 for underperformance.
INL halted central prison renovation after poor contractor performance and corruption.
DoD claims ANSF grew 73 percent since 2009 to over 340,000 personnel.
DoD states ANSF were leading over 80 percent of operations by mid-2013.
DoD says core objectives are denying al-Qaeda safe haven and preventing Taliban overthrow of the Afghan government.
State Department halted projects such as the jirga grant and prison renovation due to inadequate oversight.
ISAF's ANSF infrastructure program will end with more than 3,900 structures valued at $9.4 billion, below the originally planned $11.38 billion.
ANSF facility maintenance capacity is nascent and the MoD and MoI have too few facility engineers.
DoD obligated more than $230 million in CERP funds for over 4,000 education projects.
The Kandahar Bridging Solution increased power, and Shorandam factories grew from three in 2010 to about 66.
Afghan ministries still need training and assistance to sustain infrastructure operations and maintenance, which will be a challenge for transition.
